title: D-B-R
hookLine: davar is both a word and a thing; midbar, the desert, shares the letters

cards: Look back at this week's words. Rachamim, mercy, from the word for womb. Chen, grace.
Yada, knowing up close. Banayich read as bonayich, children as builders. Kavod, honor as weight.
Tzelem, the image in every face. Six days, each one a word on a screen and a sound in your ear. Fair question at the end of a week like that: are words just air and ink?
Hebrew answers with a root that won't keep the two apart. Dalet, bet, resh: D-B-R.

teach.b: D-B-R gives davar, and davar means two things at once: a word, and a thing. First, one verse with both: "After these things the word of the LORD came unto Abram." Things is devarim.
Word is davar. The same root twice in one line, and English needs two words to carry it. Second, a book named for it.
Deuteronomy, in Hebrew, is Devarim, from its opening: "These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel beyond the Jordan; in the wilderness." Third, that wilderness.

It's midbar, spelled with a mem in front of the same three letters. The book of Numbers is called Bemidbar, in the wilderness. Some readers hear something in that: the empty place is where the words came.
The Torah is given in the desert. Fourth, words that make things.

teach.h: BY THE WORD WERE THE HEAVENS MADE.
teach.b: "By the word of the LORD were the heavens made." In Genesis, God says, let there be light, and there is light. In this root, a word is never only air.
Once it's said, it's a thing in the world, doing something. A promise is a thing. So is an insult, so is a blessing, and so is a sentence of encouragement for a child.
This week's words were each meant to become something.

how: Jews call the fifth book of the Torah Devarim, words, and the fourth Bemidbar, in the wilderness, from words near their openings; Jewish ethics treats speech seriously, with whole bodies of law about promises, vows and harmful talk.

o: a word, and also a thing, in one Hebrew noun
a desert, the empty land the Israelites crossed
a speech given by a king to his people

s: davar can mean both a word and a thing
Genesis uses the root for both in one line: after these things, the word.
the Hebrew name of Deuteronomy means laws
it's Devarim, words, from "These are the words which Moses spoke."
midbar, wilderness, has nothing in common with davar
midbar is a mem in front of the same letters, D-B-R.

games.q: Genesis: "after these things the word of the LORD came unto Abram." in Hebrew, what are "things" and "word"?
o: the same word, just spelled backward.
games.why: devarim, things, and davar, word. Hebrew keeps the word and the thing in one root.

practice: Let the week's words pass by once, slowly, mercy, grace, knowing, builders, weight, image, and notice which one stays a little longer than the others.

Give that one a body: if it's mercy, who could use some; if it's weight, whose words could land. Picture the deed, small and specific, a call, a note, a door held open, and if you pray, carry the word into the quiet.

wordCard.voice: D-B-R. Dalet, bet, resh: davar, a word and a thing at once; the letters inside midbar, the wilderness. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a word, a thing, a matter.

carryVoice: Your line: words are things. Davar: the word and the thing, one root. A new week starts tomorrow.
